lead: This unit explains how a liquid metal is turned into a sound casting in a sand mould and in special moulds. You learn sand control, pattern allowances, moulding, gating and riser design, solidification, melting and pouring, special casting, and defect remedies. After it you can size a simple gating and riser system, read a solidification-time calculation, and choose a casting process for a part.
about: The unit moves from the mould to the finished casting. Chapter 1.1 covers sand casting and the properties that make moulding sand work: green strength, permeability, refractoriness and collapsibility. Chapter 1.2 adds patterns and the allowances that make the pattern larger than the part. Chapter 1.3 compares moulding methods and machines. Chapter 1.4 designs the gating system and riser and introduces Chvorinov's rule. Chapter 1.5 explains how the metal freezes and how solidification time scales. Chapter 1.6 covers melting and pouring practice. Chapter 1.7 compares shell, investment, die and centrifugal casting. Chapter 1.8 classifies defects and their remedies. Each chapter uses the earlier one: sand holds the mould, the pattern shapes it, gating feeds it, freezing sets the riser, and defects show what went wrong.

chapters.idea: A sand mould is a refractory sand shape that holds liquid metal until it freezes; its sand properties decide whether the mould survives.
chapters.depth: Cover sand casting layout: cope, drag, flask, sprue, runner, gate, riser, core and mould cavity. Define green sand, dry sand and loam. Explain the eight standard sand properties: green strength, dry strength, permeability, refractoriness, collapsibility, flowability, adhesiveness and durability. Give the permeability number formula P = VH/(pAt). Some syllabi call the sand foundry sand. Keep tests to the standard permeability and strength tests.

figure.title: Making a two-part sand mould
figure.aria: The steps of making a simple two-part sand mould from placing the pattern to closing the cope.

chapters.example: A standard sand specimen is 50 mm diameter and 50 mm high. 2000 cm³ of air passes through it in 2 min under a pressure of 10 g/cm². Find the permeability number. Answer: 25.5.
chapters.trap: Permeability is not porosity. Use specimen radius 2.5 cm, not diameter 5 cm, and keep pressure in g/cm²; green strength is measured while the sand is moist.
chapters.leave: Leave pattern allowances to 1.2, gating and risers to 1.4, freezing to 1.5 and defects to 1.8.

chapters.idea: A pattern is the mould-making replica of the casting, made larger by allowances so the final metal part has the required size.
chapters.depth: Cover pattern types: solid, split, match plate, cope-and-drag, sweep, skeleton and loose piece. Compare materials: wood, metal, plastic, wax and plaster. Explain the five allowances: shrinkage, draft, machining, distortion and shake or rapping; state that shake allowance is negative. Give common shrinkage values only as examples, not as universal constants. Some syllabi call this pattern making. Keep colour coding and pattern-shop details out.

figure.aria: A hierarchy of common pattern types used in sand moulding.

chapters.example: A grey cast iron block is to be 800 mm long. The shrinkage allowance is 10 mm/m. Find the pattern length. Answer: 800 + 8 = 808 mm.
chapters.trap: 10 mm/m is 1%, not 10%; draft is on vertical faces, and shake allowance is negative.
chapters.leave: Leave moulding methods to 1.3, gating to 1.4, and pattern-shop practice to workshop training.

chapters.idea: Moulding methods match the sand, flask and production rate; moulding machines replace hand ramming with jolt and squeeze actions.
chapters.depth: Cover bench, floor and pit moulding; green sand, dry sand, skin-dried, loam, CO2 and no-bake moulding. Explain jolt, squeeze, jolt-squeeze, sand slinger and flaskless moulding at principle level. Some syllabi call this moulding practice. Machine construction is taught in only a few universities; keep it short and exam-focused.

figure.title: Jolt-squeeze cycle
figure.aria: The cycle of a jolt-squeeze moulding machine from filled mould box to pattern draw.

chapters.example: A jolt-squeeze machine makes one mould in 45 s. Find the production rate in moulds per hour and per 8-hour shift. Answer: 80 moulds/h and 640 moulds/shift.
chapters.trap: Use the full cycle time, including pattern draw and closing, not only ramming time; 45 s gives 80 moulds/h, not 45.
chapters.leave: Leave special moulds to 1.7, sand tests to 1.1, and gating to 1.4.

chapters.idea: The gating system fills the mould without turbulence or slag, and the riser feeds liquid shrinkage until the casting freezes; Chvorinov's rule compares freezing times.
chapters.depth: Cover pouring basin, sprue, sprue well, runner, ingate, choke and skim bob. Explain gating ratio, pressurized and non-pressurized systems, and why the sprue is tapered. Cover top, side and blind risers; riser placement at hot spots; riser modulus. State Chvorinov's rule t = k(V/A)ⁿ with n ≈ 2, and define t, k, V and A. Some syllabi call this gating and feeding. Keep full fluid-flow derivations out.

figure.aria: A plot showing solidification time rising as the square of the volume-to-area ratio for k = 2 min/cm².

chapters.example: A casting has volume 1200 cm³ and cooling surface area 600 cm². Chvorinov's constant is k = 3 min/cm² and n = 2. Find the solidification time. A riser must solidify 1.5 times later; find the minimum V/A of the riser. Answer: t = 12 min; riser V/A = 2.45 cm.
chapters.trap: Chvorinov's A is the heat-loss surface area, not the total surface area hidden by the mould; a riser must have a larger modulus than the casting, and n is about 2, not 1.
chapters.leave: Leave the freezing mechanism to 1.5, melting to 1.6, and defect diagnosis to 1.8.

chapters.idea: A casting freezes from the mould wall inward; pure metals freeze at one temperature, alloys over a range, and the freezing range controls the zone structure and shrinkage.
chapters.depth: Cover nucleation and growth, chill zone, columnar zone and equiaxed zone. Explain directional solidification and the three shrinkages: liquid, solidification and solid. Compare pure metals and alloys with a freezing range. Apply Chvorinov's rule from 1.4 to solidification time; do not re-derive it. Some syllabi call this solidification of alloys. Keep phase diagrams to the needed freezing-range idea.

figure.aria: The zones from the mould wall to the centre of a freezing casting.

chapters.example: A 200 mm cube casting solidifies in 20 min. Using Chvorinov's rule with n = 2, find the solidification time of a 100 mm cube of the same metal in the same mould. Answer: 5 min.
chapters.trap: For the same shape, time scales with the square of size, not with volume; a 100 mm cube takes one quarter of the time, not one eighth.
chapters.leave: Leave riser sizing to 1.4, pouring temperature to 1.6, and shrinkage defects to 1.8.

chapters.idea: Melting supplies metal of the right composition and superheat; pouring delivers it cleanly at a controlled rate into the mould.
chapters.depth: Cover cupola, induction furnace, electric arc furnace and crucible furnace at principle level. Explain charge, coke, blast, slag and tap in a cupola; coil and eddy current in induction. Cover ladle treatment, pouring basin, pouring temperature and pouring speed. Only a few universities teach furnace construction details; keep this chapter short. Some syllabi call this melting and pouring practice.

figure.title: Cupola inputs and outputs
figure.aria: Inputs and outputs in a cupola from charge and blast to slag and molten metal.

chapters.example: A cupola melts 5 t of iron per hour. Find the metal charge for a 3 h shift. If coke is 12% of the metal charge, find the coke needed. Answer: 15 t metal and 1.8 t coke.
chapters.trap: Cupola uses coke and air blast, not electric arcs; low pouring temperature gives misrun, too high gives sand penetration and gas defects.
chapters.leave: Leave special casting to 1.7, gating design to 1.4, and defects to 1.8.

chapters.idea: Special casting processes use a permanent or expendable precision mould to get closer tolerances, better finish or higher production than sand casting.
chapters.depth: Cover shell moulding with resin-coated sand and a heated pattern; investment casting with wax pattern, ceramic shell and burnout; pressure die casting in hot-chamber and cold-chamber machines; centrifugal casting in true, semi-centrifugal and centrifuging modes. Compare cost, finish, size and production rate. Some syllabi call this special casting processes. Keep tooling design out.

figure.aria: A family tree of four special casting processes, with die casting split into hot- and cold-chamber types.

chapters.example: A die casting has a projected area of 80 cm². The metal pressure is 150 MPa. Find the clamping force needed. Answer: 80 cm² = 8000 mm²; force = 150 × 8000 = 1,200,000 N = 1.2 MN.
chapters.trap: Use the projected area perpendicular to the die opening, not the total surface area; 1 MPa = 1 N/mm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm².
chapters.leave: Leave sand moulding to 1.1-1.3, pouring to 1.6, and defects to 1.8.

chapters.idea: A casting defect is a recognisable failure caused by sand, pattern, gating, pouring or freezing; its shape and location point to the cause and the remedy.
chapters.depth: Cover blowhole, porosity, shrinkage cavity, hot tear, cold shut, misrun, slag inclusion, sand inclusion, scab, swell, drop, mismatch, core shift, penetration and runout. Group by cause and give one remedy each. Some syllabi call this casting defects and remedies. Keep inspection methods to a mention; NDT belongs to later study.

figure.aria: Common casting defects grouped by their main cause: sand, pouring, freezing and pattern.

chapters.example: A foundry makes 500 castings in a shift. 35 are rejected. Find the rejection rate and the yield of good castings. Answer: rejection 7%; good castings 93%.
chapters.trap: A shrinkage cavity has a rough, dendritic internal surface; a blowhole is smooth and round. Hot tears form while the casting is hot and contracting, not after it is cold.
chapters.leave: Leave welding defects to Unit 4 and machining defects to Unit 5.
